chunks: I am not going to offer my excuse for reproving him for (some of) his innovations, for if my good counsel and guidance to him was a sin then very often a person who is blamed has no sin and “sometimes the only reward a counseller reaps is suspicion (of evil)”.

key_terms.أَحْدَاثاً: innovations (plural of bid'ah, referring to religious innovations)

ai.seo_question: What is the relationship between blame and sin when offering guidance or criticizing innovations?
ai.summary: In this response to Muawiya, Imam Ali (AS) employs the rhetorical device of *istihlal al-madhh* (justifying the fault) to counter accusations of envy (*tanammur*), asserting that if the act of guiding others is deemed a crime, then the advisor is often unfairly blamed despite having no actual sin. This highlights the historical tension between Ali’s direct, principled criticism and Muawiya’s political maneuvering, where the truth-teller is often suspected of ulterior motives. The phrase 'the sincere advisor may still be suspected' underscores the scholarly principle that *nasihah* (sincere counsel) does not guarantee acceptance, reflecting the broader Shia view of the Imam’s role as a guide who bears the burden of truth regardless of reception.
